summary: Direct proportion means two quantities keep a constant ratio: multiply one by k and the other is multiplied by k, so the graph is a straight line through the origin (y = kx). Inverse proportion means the product is constant: multiply one by k and the other is divided by k (xy = c, a decreasing curve). The core learning goals are (1) making the multiplicative structure of direct proportion explicit, distinct from merely additive change, and (2) resisting the 'illusion of proportionality' — the reflex to treat every relationship as directly proportional. Learners should habitually ASK whether doubling one quantity really doubles the other, halves it, or does neither.
misconceptions: Illusion of proportionality — treating every relationship as directly proportional, applying y=kx to situations that are linear-but-not-proportional (phone plan with a fixed charge) or inverse.
Confusing direct and inverse: expecting 'twice as fast' to mean 'twice the time' rather than half the time.
Additive rather than multiplicative scaling: going from 4 pens to 8 pens by adding the same amount to the cost instead of doubling it.
Believing any straight-line graph shows direct proportion, ignoring whether it passes through the origin.

activities.title: Proportion lab: drive one quantity, watch the other
steps: Work with three switchable scenarios: pens & cost (4 pens £6 → 10 pens £15, directly proportional); taps filling a bucket or workers digging a hole (inversely proportional); and a phone plan of £15/month + £0.20/min (linear but NOT proportional).
Before changing anything, PREDICT where the next point will land on the graph and what the paired value should be — write or say the prediction and your reason first.
Change quantity A (e.g. with a slider or by choosing a new value) and watch quantity B recompute, with the point plotting live on a graph while a ratio table fills in alongside.

In the phone-plan scenario, double the minutes while predicting the cost will also double; observe that the plotted point lands below your prediction and the traced line clearly does NOT pass through the origin.
In the inverse scenario, halve the number of taps and observe the fill time double, with the curve bending away from the straight line you expected.

Apply two quick tests out loud: 'if one quantity is zero, is the other zero?' (a first check for direct proportion; it is needed but not enough by itself, so also confirm that the ratio stays constant) and 'does doubling one halve the other, keeping the product the same?' (inverse-proportion test).
activities.insight: Quantity B's response to driving quantity A reveals the structure: in direct proportion the ratio holds (and the line goes through the origin), in inverse proportion the product holds (one goes down as the other goes up), and in linear-but-not-proportional situations a fixed charge means the line misses the origin so doubling fails. Proportionality is a property to test, not a default to assume.

activities.title: Sort situations into direct, inverse, or neither
steps: Sort six real-world situations into three bins: directly proportional, inversely proportional, or neither.

For each, justify the placement with a test: for direct proportion, check that the ratio stays constant (so doubling one doubles the other, and zero gives zero); for inverse, check that the product stays constant (so doubling one halves the other). 'Zero gives zero' alone is not enough: a square's side and its area both start at zero, but they are not proportional.
Choose which of several graphs shows direct proportion, deliberately comparing a straight line through the origin against a straight line that misses the origin.
Complete a ratio table for a directly proportional situation by multiplying (scaling columns), and check whether an answer found by adding a fixed difference gives the same result.
activities.insight: Classifying situations and matching them to graphs forces the discrimination that defines the topic: not every straight line is proportional (it must pass through the origin), and additive scaling is not the same as multiplicative scaling.

activities.title: Reference triptych: three graphs, three tests
steps: Study a labelled set of three graphs side by side: a straight line through the origin (direct), a smooth decreasing curve (inverse), and a straight line that misses the origin (linear but not proportional).
Reveal, for each graph, its defining property — 'does the line start at (0,0)?' for the lines and 'does the product stay the same?' for the curve.
Use the triptych as a consolidation reference while classifying new situations, checking origin behaviour as a fast first diagnostic.
activities.insight: For straight-line graphs, origin behaviour is a quick diagnostic: through the origin means direct proportion, and missing the origin means linear but not proportional. A decreasing curve should prompt a check of whether the product stays constant, because not every decreasing curve shows inverse proportion.

activities.title: Predict–observe–explain with two taps
steps: PREDICT: One tap fills a bucket in 60 seconds. If you open a SECOND tap of the same flow, how long to fill the same bucket? Write your time AND your reason before testing.
OBSERVE: in the idealised model (each tap gives the same constant flow, the bucket volume is fixed, nothing overflows), two taps fill it in 30 seconds.

EXPLAIN: why the naive 'still 60' or '120 seconds' prediction is wrong — twice the taps gives HALF the time because taps and time are inversely proportional: the bucket's volume (total water) is fixed and each tap has equal flow, so the number of taps × the fill time stays constant, meaning doubling the taps halves the time.

Then tackle the phone-plan question: a plan costs £15/month plus £0.20 per minute. Sam says 'if I talk for twice as many minutes, my bill will be twice as big.' Decide whether Sam is right and explain how you know.

Probe deeper: What would Sam pay for 0 minutes, and what does that say about proportionality? Work out the bill for 100 minutes and for 200 minutes — is the second exactly double the first? What if the plan had no £15 charge — would Sam be right then? And is 'twice as many taps' the same kind of relationship as the phone bill?
activities.insight: Stating a reason before observing exposes the illusion of proportionality: a learner who truly grasps direct proportion tests the origin ('what happens at zero?') and sees that the fixed charge breaks the doubling rule, while a learner running the reflex answers 'twice the bill' automatically.

checkQuestion: A phone plan costs £15 each month plus £0.20 for every minute you call. Sam says: 'If I talk for twice as many minutes, my bill will be twice as big.' Is Sam right? Explain how you know.
checkAnswer: Sam is wrong. The bill is NOT directly proportional to the minutes because of the fixed £15 charge: at 0 minutes the bill is £15, not £0, so the relationship does not pass through the origin. Doubling the minutes doubles only the £0.20-per-minute part, not the whole bill — e.g. 100 min costs £35, but 200 min costs £55, which is less than double.
